The Puerto Rico government put my completely solvent bank into receivership under the pretense of protecting customers, who needed no protection at all, as there was more than enough cash in the bank to repay every customer in full. But now, thanks to the government's "help," customers need protection from the Receiver.

The Receiver was put in charge of my bank over four years ago. Over that time, he has paid a total of 78 customer claims out of thousands of customers, including the 27 he paid in Q2 of 2026. During that quarter, he paid himself $109,732 and paid another $59,242 in bills the bank supposedly incurred, despite it not being in business. The total spent over the quarter was $168,974 to pay just 27 claims. That's two claims per week, at an average cost of $6,260 per claim.

Despite the bank having over 3,500 customers when it went into receivership, the Receiver only recognizes 679 claims. I guess the rest of the customers will just lose everything. Before the government organized publicity falsely accusing the bank of facilitating tax evasion and money laundering in the fall of 2020, it had over 8,000 customers. At least most customers withdrew their money before the government stepped in to "protect" them.

This means that after four years and three months, only 2.2% of the bank's customers have been paid. At the rate at which the Receiver settled claims in the most recent quarter, if he pays the remaining 601 claims he admits are outstanding at the same pace, it will take over five and a half more years to finish the job. During that time, the Receiver will pay himself another $2.44 million.

However, since June 30, 2022, the Receiver has spent a total of $2,192,989, including $863,517 paid to himself. Since only 78 claims have been paid in total over that time, the total cost per paid claim is over $28,000! This is despite the governing liquidation order requiring the bank “to be liquidated in the most efficient and inexpensive way possible.”

This is a total racket. The Puerto Rican government has allowed the Receiver to turn my bank into his personal piggy bank. The worst part of this travesty is that there was no legitimate regulatory reason to shut down the bank. Even if there was, there was no financial reason to put it in receivership. It was all a PR stunt so OCIF, the IRS, and the J5 could take false credit for stopping tax evasion and money laundering, despite knowing that my bank facilitated neither of those crimes. 

It's hard to imagine a better example of government corruption than what is happening in Puerto Rico to my bank. Let this serve as a warning to anyone outside of Puerto Rico looking to set up an offshore bank. Stay away from Puerto Rico. If you happen to have any money in a Puerto Rican bank, withdraw it now while you still can.
